### [Prelims Source Page 161](pages/prelims/prelims_page_161.pdf)

- The ceiling binds the candidate, never the party: the most repeated trap in this area.
- Travel by a party’s star campaigners is not counted against the candidate.
- The ceiling is set by the Central Government, not the ECI.
Contributions (RPA, 1951)
- Sec 29C: Contributions above ₹20,000 are reported to the ECI to claim income tax exemption (Sec 13A, Income
Tax Act).
- Sec 29B: Parties may accept contributions from any person or company except a government company; foreign
sources are barred (FCRA, 2010), though the Finance Acts of 2016 and 2018 retrospectively let Indian subsidiaries
of foreign companies donate.
- Cash is capped at ₹2,000 per donor (Finance Act, 2017); electoral trusts since 2013.
- Companies (Sec 182, Companies Act, 2013): At least 3 years old, giving up to 7.5% of average net profits.
Traps
- Failure to file the contribution report costs the tax exemption; it does not deregister the party.
- Amounts below ₹20,000 need not be itemised, which is how large “unknown” income persists.
- Government companies and companies under 3 years old cannot contribute at all.
Electoral bonds struck down (ADR v Union of India, 15 February 2024)
- A unanimous five judge Constitution Bench (CJI D.Y. Chandrachud) struck down the Electoral Bond Scheme, 2018
and the enabling amendments to the RPA, 1951, the Companies Act, 2013 (which had removed the 7.5% cap and
the duty to disclose) and the Income Tax Act, 1961.
- Grounds: The voter’s right to information under Art 19(1)(a), and manifest arbitrariness under Art 14 in allowing
unlimited corporate donations, even by loss making companies.
- SBI was told to stop issuing bonds and report the details to the ECI by March 2024.
Traps
- Bonds were issued only by SBI, as bearer instruments valid for 15 days, carrying no interest, and were introduced
through the Finance Act, 2017 as a Money Bill.
NOMINATION, POLL AND COUNTING
Nomination and scrutiny (RPA, 1951)
- Proposers: A recognised National or State party candidate needs one; anyone else, including a registered
unrecognised party’s candidate, needs ten (or one tenth of the electors, if fewer).
- Up to 4 nomination papers. The Returning Officer may reject only for disqualification, non compliance with the
nomination or deposit rules, or a non genuine signature; defects not of a substantial character are ignored.
Traps
- The one proposer concession comes with recognition, not registration.
- Improper rejection voids the election, but only through an election petition after the result, never a writ.
Security deposit (Secs 34, 158)
- Lok Sabha ₹25,000 (₹12,500 for SC/ST); Assembly or Council ₹10,000 (₹5,000 for SC/ST); paid with the
nomination.
- Forfeited unless the candidate polls more than one sixth of the total valid votes; returned if he withdraws in time,
his nomination is rejected, or he dies before the poll.
Traps
- The test is one sixth of the total valid votes polled, not of the winner’s votes.
Two constituency cap (Sec 33(7)) [PRELIMS 2021]
- Since the RP (Amendment) Act, 1996, no one may contest more than two constituencies in a general election, a
group of by elections or biennial elections; this covers the Lok Sabha, Assembly, Rajya Sabha and Council.
- Elected from both, he must resign one within 14 days, or both fall vacant; the vacated seat goes to a by election.
Traps
- Devi Lal contested three seats in 1991, which was lawful before the cap.

---

### [Prelims Source Page 162](pages/prelims/prelims_page_162.pdf)

- The ECI’s proposal that the candidate pay ₹5 lakh (Assembly) or ₹10 lakh (Lok Sabha) towards the by election is not
law; the Supreme Court (2023) refused to strike down the two seat option and left it to Parliament.
First past the post and NOTA
- Simple plurality decides Lok Sabha, Assembly and local body seats; there is no 50% threshold and no run off.
- PUCL v Union of India (27 September 2013): Abstaining must stay secret (Art 19(1)(a)), so the Court directed a
NOTA button; first used in the 2013 Assembly elections and placed on the ballot through the Conduct of Election
Rules.
Traps
- NOTA is not a right to reject: if it polls highest, the leading candidate still wins, with no repoll.
- No NOTA in Rajya Sabha and Council elections (Shailesh Manubhai Parmar, 2018).
- The President, Vice President, Rajya Sabha and Councils are elected by proportional representation by single
transferable vote, where a quota must be crossed.
EVMs and VVPAT
- Statutory backing: Sec 61A, RPA 1951, from 15 March 1989; EVMs in all 543 seats from 2004.
- First pilot: Paravur, Kerala (1982), set aside in A.C. Jose (1984) for want of statutory backing.
- VVPAT: Added through the Conduct of Election Rules, 1961 (14 August 2013) after Subramanian Swamy v ECI
(2013); first used in Noksen, Nagaland (2013). Since 2019, slips from 5 random polling stations per constituency or
segment are counted.
- ADR v ECI (26 April 2024): Rejected 100% VVPAT counting and a return to paper ballots; ordered Symbol Loading
Units to be sealed and stored after results.
Traps
- VVPAT comes from the Rules, not the Act.
- EVMs are standalone, not networked, and made only by BEL and ECIL.
By elections (Sec 151A)
- A casual vacancy is filled within six months, unless less than one year of the term remains.
- The member serves only the unexpired term, not a fresh five years.
Traps
- Both conditions matter: with less than a year left, no by election need be held.
CAMPAIGN REGULATION AND ELECTORAL OFFENCES
Model Code of Conduct
- No statute: Evolved by consensus among parties and enforced by the ECI under Art 324; traces to a code drawn up
in Kerala, 1960.
- In force from the announcement of the schedule until the election process is complete; binds parties, candidates
and the party in power.
- Eight parts: General conduct, meetings, processions, polling day, polling booths, observers, the party in power,
election manifestos.
Traps
- It has no penalty of its own: it bites through censure, campaign bans or Art 324 powers. Conduct that is also an
offence is punished under the BNS or the RPA, 1951.
- The ECI has itself opposed making it statutory, preferring speed to litigation.
Silence period and exit polls (Secs 126, 126A)
- Silence period: In the 48 hours ending with the close of poll in an area, no public meeting or procession, and no
election matter on cinema, television or similar apparatus.
- Exit polls: None conducted or published from the start of the poll in the first phase until half an hour after the close
of the last phase (RP (Amendment) Act, 2009).
Traps
- The silence period does not cover print media, and it runs constituency wise, so it differs by phase.
- Exit polls are banned by statute; opinion polls are not, except during the 48 hour silence.
- The exit poll window is notified by the ECI and can run for weeks.

---

### [Prelims Source Page 163](pages/prelims/prelims_page_163.pdf)

Corrupt practices and electoral offences
- Corrupt practices (Sec 123, RPA 1951): Bribery, undue influence, appeal on grounds of religion, race, caste,
community or language, promoting enmity, false statements about a candidate’s personal character, hiring
vehicles for voters, expenditure beyond the ceiling, booth capturing, and seeking help from government servants.
- Electoral offences (RPA, 1951): Disorderly conduct at meetings (Sec 127), canvassing within 100 metres of a
polling station (Sec 130), booth capturing (Sec 135A).
- The RPA, 1950 has only two offences, false declaration and breach of official duty, both about the roll.
Traps
- A corrupt practice voids the election and can disqualify; an electoral offence is punished as a crime. Booth
capturing is both.
- Abhiram Singh v C.D. Commachen (2017): An appeal to the voter’s religion is as much a corrupt practice as an
appeal to the candidate’s.
DISPUTES AND WHO DECIDES WHAT
Election petitions (Art 329(b); RPA, 1951)
- An election to Parliament or a State Legislature can be questioned only by an election petition in the High Court
(single judge), within 45 days of the result.
- Grounds (Sec 100): Disqualification of the winner, corrupt practice, improper acceptance or rejection of a
nomination, or non compliance materially affecting the result.
- Outcomes: Dismissal; the election declared void; another candidate declared elected; persons guilty of corrupt
practice named. Appeal lies to the Supreme Court within 30 days (Sec 116A).
- “Election” covers the whole process from notification to result; no writ lies midway, even for wrongful rejection of a
nomination (N.P. Ponnuswami, 1952).
Traps
- Before notification, writ jurisdiction is open. The Art 329(a) bar covers only delimitation laws and orders, so ordinary
ECI decisions remain open to writ.
- Art 329(b) names no court; the High Court hears petitions because the RPA, 1951 says so. Election Tribunals were
abolished in 1966.
- President and Vice President election disputes go directly to the Supreme Court (Art 71).

---

### [Prelims Source Page 164](pages/prelims/prelims_page_164.pdf)

![Elections: Who Decides What (Disqualification & Disputes Matrix)](diagrams/pre_diag_elections_who_decides_what_p164.png)
*Diagram Screenshot: [Elections: Who Decides What (Disqualification & Disputes Matrix)](diagrams/pre_diag_elections_who_decides_what_p164.png) | [Full Source Page 164](pages/prelims/prelims_page_164.pdf)*

Who decides what
- Election dispute: High Court.
- Disqualification of a sitting member: President/Governor, on the ECI’s binding opinion.
- Defection: Speaker/Chairman.
- Election schedule: ECI.
- Splits, mergers and symbol disputes: ECI.
- Delimitation: Delimitation Commission; its orders are immune from courts.
- Expenditure ceiling: Central Government, by rules.
- Registration and recognition of parties: ECI.

### [Smash Mains Source Page 165](pages/mains/mains_page_165.pdf)

Key Legal Provisions Regulating Political Funding

#### A. Representation of the People Act (RPA), 1951
1. Section 29B: Entitles political parties to accept voluntary contributions from any person or company
(excluding foreign sources and government companies).
2. Section 29C: Mandates parties to report all donations exceeding ₹20,000 to the Election Commission
(ECI) annually. If they fail to report, they lose tax exemptions.
3. Section 77: Requires every candidate to keep a separate and correct account of all expenditure incurred
between the date of nomination and the date of declaration of result.

#### B. Income Tax Act, 1961
1. Section 13A: Grants 100% tax exemption to political parties on their income (from house property,
voluntary contributions, capital gains) provided they:
a. Maintain detailed books of account.
b. Record the name and address of every person who contributes more than ₹20,000.
c. Do not accept cash donations exceeding ₹2,000.

#### C. Companies Act, 2013
1. Section 182: Regulates corporate funding.
a. Pre-2017: Companies could only donate up to 7.5% of their average net profits.
b. Post-2017: The 7.5% cap was removed, allowing unlimited corporate funding.
2. Any donation must be authorized by a resolution passed by the Board of Directors.

#### D. Foreign Contribution Regulation Act (FCRA), 2010
1. Political parties and candidates are strictly prohibited from accepting foreign contributions.
2. 2016/2018 Retroactive Amendment: The definition of "foreign source" was changed to exempt
Indian-owned subsidiaries of foreign companies.
In Association for Democratic Reforms & Anr. v. Union of India & Ors Case, a 5-judge bench struck down the
Electoral Bond Scheme as unconstitutional (). The court ruled that:
- It violated the Voter's Right to Information under Article 19(1)(a).
- The Anonymity provided by the bonds allowed for secret corruption and "crony capitalism."
- Amendments to the Companies Act (allowing unlimited funding) and the RPA (exempting bond
reporting) were also declared void.
Issues:
1. Involvement of black money: According to SBI data on Electoral Bonds (EBs)-
2. 41 firms which donated ₹2,471 crore to the ruling party at centre under the EBs scheme are facing probe
by government agencies
3. At least 30 shell companies purchased electoral bonds worth over ₹143 crore.
4. Weak Regulation - The Election Commission of India (ECI) has limited power to audit or penalize
parties for funding violations.
5. Uncapped Party Expenditure: While individual candidates have spending limits, political parties can
spend unlimited amounts on campaigns.
6. Institutionalized Quid Pro Quo: Removing corporate donation caps (7.5% of profits) has led to fears of
"policy-for-funding swaps" and crony capitalism
7. "Unknown" Income Streams: Parties exploit the ₹20,000 threshold to keep a massive chunk of their
income anonymous. Eg. 65% of regional party funds come from "unknown sources."
167

---

### [Smash Mains Source Page 166](pages/mains/mains_page_166.pdf)

8. Rise of Shadow Funding: Funds are increasingly diverted to "IT Cells" and "Third-party" social media
campaigners without disclosure.
9. Inequitable Funding Distribution: Corporate donations are heavily skewed toward the ruling party. In
2024-25, the BJP received 83% of all donations made through Electoral Trusts.
10. Foreign Influence Risks: Retroactive FCRA amendments allow foreign-owned Indian subsidiaries to
fund parties, risking national sovereignty.
11. Inadequate Audit Mechanism: Parties choose their own private auditors, leading to potential "friendly
audits" and lack of rigor.
Way Forward:
1. ECI has suggested that parties should be made to disclose contributions received in cash for smaller
sums in case they exceed 20% of total funds raised.
2. Lower Disclosure Threshold: Reduce the anonymous donation limit from ₹20,000 to ₹2,000.
3. Real-time Digital Disclosure: Use the IEMS portal (2026) to mandate uploading of every donation over
₹2,000 within 48 hours.
4. Cap on Party Expenditure: Amend the RPA, 1951 to impose a statutory limit on total party spending
(Law Commission 255th Report).
5. Partial State Funding (In-Kind): Provide facilities like fuel, airtime, and paper instead of cash to parties
(Indrajit Gupta Committee).
6. National Election Fund: Establish a central pool where corporates donate; the ECI then distributes funds
based on vote share.
7. CAG-Approved Audits: Mandate that all political party accounts be audited by a panel of auditors
approved by the CAG.
8. Global Best Practice (Germany): Adopt the "Parteienfinanzierung" model where public funds are
allocated based on verified vote shares.
9. Re-implement the cap on corporate donations to prevent "shell company" influence.
10. Bring political parties formally under the RTI for all financial and donor-related queries.
11. Enforce Campaign Expenditure Limits
a. Monitor actual spending on social media ads, surrogate advertising, influencers etc.
b. Link expenditure data to election affidavits and IT returns
One Nation One Election
ONOE refers to the proposal to synchronize the timing of all elections in India to occur within a single
timeframe or cycle.
History of ONOE
1. Simultaneous elections were the norm in India for the first four general election cycles (1952, 1957, 1962,
and 1967).
2. The cycle was broken due to the premature dissolution of several State Assemblies in 1968 and 1969,
followed by the dissolution of the Lok Sabha in 1970 and fresh polls in 1971.
3. The Law Commission (170th Report, 1999) and the Parliamentary Standing Committee (2015) strongly
advocated for returning to simultaneous polls to ensure governance stability.
Key Benefits of One Nation One Election
1. Reduced Financial Burden for the exchequer - costs of logistics, polling staff, and security.
2. Continuity in Governance: Prevents "policy paralysis" caused by the frequent imposition of the Model
Code of Conduct (MCC).
168

---

### [Smash Mains Source Page 167](pages/mains/mains_page_167.pdf)

3. Reduced Administrative Strain: Teachers and police officers can focus on their primary duties rather
than frequent election duty.
4. Higher Voter Turnout: Consolidating elections reduces "voter fatigue" and encourages citizens to vote
for all tiers at once.
5. Curbing Black Money: Limits the opportunities for political parties to raise and spend unaccounted cash
in multiple cycles.
6. Focus on Long-term Policy: Parties can focus on nation-building for five years rather than staying in
"perpetual campaign mode."
7. Social Cohesion: Reduces frequency of communal or caste-based mobilization during election periods.
8. Supply Chain Stability: Minimizes disruptions to businesses and production cycles caused by frequent
holidays and rallies.
9. Predictable Investment Climate: Stability in governance timelines provides certainty to global
investors regarding policy consistency.
10. Efficiency for Parties: Smaller parties save on repetitive campaigning, allowing a more level playing
field against wealthy national parties.
Major Challenges in One Nation One Election
1. Constitutional Amendments: Requires amending Articles 83, 85, 172, and 174, which require political
consensus.
2. Impact on Federalism: Critics argue it undermines state autonomy by making regional polls subservient
to the national narrative.
3. Voter Confusion: Simultaneous polls might lead to voters mixing up local, state, and national issues.
4. A state might face frequent mid-term polls as, if a government falls mid-term, the replacement would
only serve the "unexpired term.
5. Logistical issue: ECI would need nearly double the current inventory of machines to support 1 million+
booths.
6. Regional Issues Sidelined: National security or foreign policy can overshadow local issues like water or
electricity.
7. Accountability Deficit: Voters only get to "punish" or "reward" politicians once in five years rather than
more frequently.
8. Security Deployment: Providing high-level security for all booths across India simultaneously is a
massive paramilitary challenge.
9. Judicial Workload: A surge in election petitions all at once could overwhelm the High Courts.
Key Provisions of the ONOE Bill
1. Article 82A (Appointed Date): The President will notify an "Appointed Date" (expected after 2024 polls)
to trigger the synchronization.
2. Article 83 & 172 Amendments: Stipulates that if the Lok Sabha or Assembly is dissolved prematurely, the
new House serves only the unexpired term.
3. Phased Implementation:
a. Phase 1: Simultaneous elections for Lok Sabha and State Assemblies.
b. Phase 2: Local body (Panchayat/Municipality) elections to be held within 100 days of the general
polls.
4. Common Electoral Roll: Amendment to Article 325 to allow ECI to prepare a single roll for all three tiers
of government.
Way Forward
1. Building Consensus: Engage with regional parties through the Joint Parliamentary Committee to
address federalism concerns.
2. Scale up the production of M3-version EVMs to meet the massive simultaneous demand.
3. Explore the German "Constructive Vote of No Confidence" model to prevent premature dissolutions.
4. Voter Education: nationwide awareness drive to help voters distinguish between local and national
issues.
169

---

### [Smash Mains Source Page 168](pages/mains/mains_page_168.pdf)

5. Administrative Audit: Conduct a dry run in 4-5 states before the 2029 national rollout.
6. Judicial Benches: Set up special election tribunals to resolve all disputes from a single cycle within six
months.
7. Indrajit Gupta Recommendations: Combine ONOE with partial state funding to further reduce the
influence of black money.
170
